title: TanawPamana: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models on Philippine Cultural Heritage Sites
summary: A multimodal benchmark for evaluating VLMs on Philippine cultural heritage site recognition and knowledge. Accepted to O-COCOSDA 2026.
description: Vision-language models are increasingly used to identify and describe places, yet their recognition and knowledge of specific cultures remain poorly understood, particularly in underrepresented regions such as the Philippines. This study introduces the Tanawpamana Dataset, a repository of Philippine heritage site images with metadata based on the Talapamana registry of the National Commission for Culture and the Arts of the Philippines. We also introduce the Tanawpamana Benchmark, comprising 4,046 tasks designed to evaluate models' recognition and knowledge of heritage sites. Evaluating seven vision-language models, we find that they struggle more with fine-grained visual discrimination among similar heritage sites than with coarse recognition, and that their geographic knowledge is weaker when inferred from image inputs than from text.
thought: This started during my research internship at NAIST in Japan, under the thorough advisement of Ouchi-sensei and the support of Sakti-sensei. After the internship, I took it independently and saw it through to publication. Proud solo work.

title: TDR: Tagalog Diacritic Restoration Dataset
coauthors: L.R. Fermin, Z.A. Africa, R.I. Flores
summary: A dataset and evaluation protocols for automatic restoration of diacritical marks in Tagalog text. Accepted to O-COCOSDA 2026.
description: Homographs are words that share identical spelling but differ in meaning and pronunciation. In Tagalog, these distinctions are disambiguated through tuldik (diacritical marks), which are rarely preserved in contemporary text. This scarcity limits diacritic restoration, a capability useful for downstream tasks such as prosody selection in text-to-speech synthesis. TDR is an annotated corpus of 40 frequent Tagalog homographs constructed from news text, alongside a collocation-driven retrieval method to expand the dataset and reduce class imbalance among minor variants. We show that TDR supplies a capability absent from pretrained models, and that this capability can be learned by small, inexpensive models as well as fine-tuned LLMs.
thought: My undergraduate thesis. I really pushed to get it published because I did not want to live with the what-ifs.

title: PACUTE: Phonology-, Affix-, and Character-level Understanding of Tokens for Filipino
coauthors: J.R. Montalan, D.D. Africa, J.P. Layacan, R.I. Flores, L.C. Gamboa
summary: A diagnostic benchmark that tests whether LLMs understand Filipino word structure: infixes, reduplication, and diacritics.
description: Large language models process text as sequences of subword tokens, which can obscure the character-level and morphological structure underlying word formation. This limitation is most acute for languages with non-concatenative morphology, where standard tokenizers systematically misalign token boundaries with morpheme boundaries. PACUTE is a diagnostic benchmark of 4,600 tasks designed to evaluate morphological understanding in Filipino, a language with productive infixation, reduplication, and diacritic-driven lexical distinctions typically absent from written text. It includes a hierarchical diagnostic framework of six compositional levels that localizes where morphological understanding breaks down. Open-weight models perform near chance on morpheme decomposition regardless of scale. Frontier models perform much better, often recovering individual affixes, but remain far below their character-level ceilings on compositional tasks. These results identify productive morphological composition, not character access alone, as the persistent bottleneck for Filipino word-structure understanding.
thought: This was my first time collaborating as an independent researcher with more experienced people in the field. I looked up to all of them as mentor figures.

title: FilSwitch: A Filipino-English Code-Switched Speech Dataset
coauthors: S. Angeles, E. Panugayan, C. Cheng, T. Tiam-Lee
summary: A read-speech dataset for evaluating and adapting ASR systems to Filipino-English code-switching. Accepted to O-COCOSDA 2026.
description: Filipino-English code-switching (Taglish) is widespread in the Philippines but largely absent from ASR training data. FilSwitch is a read-speech dataset of 3,513 utterances (8.9 hours) recorded by 152 speakers. News-derived sentences were filtered for code-switching, readability, and appropriateness, then manually validated and transcript-normalized. Among tested models, fine-tuning Whisper on the dataset reduced word error rate from 13.62% to 9.24%, demonstrating the value of domain-matched data for Taglish ASR.
thought: Worked with Sherwynn, whom I met during my internship at NAIST.

title: Last Translation Benchmark
coauthors: V. Zouhar, N. Bafna, M. Choudhary, M. Züfle, S. Rajaee, P. Chen, J. Vamvas, et al.
summary: A benchmark for evaluating the upper limits of machine translation quality. Dataset contributor.
description: Machine translation has improved dramatically, but it remains unclear what the ceiling actually looks like. This benchmark attempts to define and measure that upper bound, drawing on contributed datasets from researchers across multiple languages and contexts.
thought: Fun to be a contributor to an open source study like this.

title: We Are Convinced That Persuasion is Linear and Bilingual in LLMs
summary: Tests whether persuasion is represented as a single linear direction inside LLMs, and whether this transfers cross-lingually between English and Tagalog.
description: LLM chatbots now carry substantial persuasive power, yet little is known about whether persuasion is a structured internal property of these models. Using diff-of-means activation analysis on Zeng et al.'s persuasion taxonomy, we find five techniques converge on a single linear direction (minimum pairwise cosine similarity 0.77), causally sufficient to increase judged persuasiveness via activation steering (44.4 to 51.3 mean score). We also test causal cross-lingual transfer: steering with English-derived directions on Tagalog prompts and vice versa, both show increased persuasiveness and high cross-lingual representational similarity (0.66 average cosine similarity). Submitted to the APART Global South AI Safety Hackathon.
thought: The title is an obvious play on words: convinced, persuasion. But honestly, I am not convinced anymore. The paper has obvious limitations. Still, it was meaningful work. A three-day hackathon I pushed through even on the day of my graduation, and my first real attempt at mechanistic interpretability.

title: Graph-Based Analysis of Customer-Merchant Payment Networks
summary: Models customer-merchant payment data as a bipartite graph and introduces the Merchant Importance Score to capture distinctive customer preferences.
description: Conventional transaction analysis based on frequency or total spending often misses how distinctively a customer prefers a particular merchant. This study models customer-merchant payment data as a bipartite graph and introduces the Merchant Importance Score (MIS), an edge-weighting scheme that captures how uniquely important a merchant is to a customer relative to others. Applied to Private Wealth customers of BPI, MIS-based analysis reveals a behavioral pattern concentrated in upscale dining that simpler methods miss. The study also incorporates MIS-derived similarity profiles into a graph neural network to surface non-PW customers with high affinity for the PW segment.
thought: My master's capstone. It was my first experience working long-term with a client, and the closest thing I had to a real professional relationship before entering industry.

title: BEA: Blue Eagle Assistant
summary: A multi-agent AI chatbot that answers student questions using Ateneo handbook references and university policies.
description: Ateneo students lack a fast, policy-aware assistant for navigating university handbooks and contacts. BEA is an AI-powered chatbot built with Streamlit that answers student questions using handbook references, university policies, and contact information. Final project for PSI AI Academy, an AI engineering course.

title: SIMS: Social Impact Mapping Simulation
summary: Simulates two-party elections where voters shift stance over time based on social influence.
description: Two-party elections involve complex social influence dynamics that simple models fail to capture. SIMS is a Java-based election simulation with a GUI, where simulated voters are placed on a social network and choose between two political parties. Each voter's stance can shift over time based on the influence of nearby voters, grounded in Social Impact Theory (Nowak, Szamrej & Latané, 1990).
